name: Barabbas
source_summary: A convicted insurrectionist and murderer imprisoned in Jerusalem, released by Pilate at the crowd's demand in place of Jesus during the Passover custom of freeing a prisoner.
family_friendly_summary: Barabbas was a prisoner in Jerusalem who had been involved in a rebellion against Rome and had committed murder. It was a custom at Passover for the Roman governor to release one prisoner chosen by the crowd as a gesture of goodwill. Pilate, the governor, tried offering the crowd a choice between releasing Jesus or releasing Barabbas, likely hoping the people would choose to free Jesus, since he could find no real guilt in Him. Instead, stirred up by the religious leaders, the crowd shouted for Barabbas to be released and for Jesus to be crucified instead. Pilate gave in to the pressure, and Barabbas walked free while Jesus took his place, condemned to die on the cross. Barabbas's story is a vivid, real-life picture of the innocent Jesus dying in place of the guilty.
adult_story: Barabbas was a notorious prisoner, described as an insurrectionist who had committed murder during a rebellion, held in custody in Jerusalem at the time of Jesus's trial (Mark 15:7; Luke 23:19). It was customary for the Roman governor to release one prisoner chosen by the crowd during the Passover festival, and Pilate, recognizing Jesus's innocence and likely hoping to avoid executing Him, offered the crowd a choice between Jesus, "called Christ," and Barabbas (Matthew 27:15-18). Some manuscripts of Matthew preserve Barabbas's full name as "Jesus Barabbas," meaning "son of the father" -- a detail, if original, that would sharpen an already stark irony: the crowd was asked to choose between a false "son of the father" guilty of real violence and the true Son of the Father who was innocent (27:16-17). Stirred up by the chief priests and elders, the crowd demanded Barabbas's release and Jesus's crucifixion; Pilate, unable or unwilling to resist the pressure, granted their demand (27:20-26). Barabbas simply walked free, his guilt never atoned for by his own suffering, while the innocent Jesus was condemned to die in the very manner Barabbas himself might have faced for his crimes. Scripture records nothing further of Barabbas's life afterward, but his release stands as one of the Gospels' most direct, literal pictures of substitution -- an innocent man dying so a guilty one could go free.
devotionals: Barabbas’s story teaches us about substitution; may we look to Jesus, whose grace and truth never fail.
Through Barabbas’s experience of the innocent for the guilty, God teaches us to trust His wisdom and follow Jesus faithfully.
